extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy of science, and argumentation/inductive reasoning
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and guidance for judging the strength and scope of inductive, analogical, and causal inferences (when they may be extended in time/place, how analogy compares to induction, and what warrants treating hypotheses as guides to experiment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Extend derivative laws only to adjacent cases
rubrics_metrics.description: This extension of derivative laws, not causative, beyond the limits of observation can only be to adjacent cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Probability that a derivative law holds decreases the further one projects it in time or place; e.g., the high warrant for expecting the sun to rise to-morrow does not extend with the same assurance to twenty thousand years hence because new cumulative effects or rare combinations of causes might intervene. Hence extend derivative (non-causal) generalizations only to cases adjacent in time or circumstances; confidence abates with distance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causal knowledge permits wider and firmer extension than mere empirical laws
rubrics_metrics.description: When we know the causes ... we can now [extend] to cases more distant in time or place than when the uniformity had been known only as an empirical law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowing the actual causes (e.g., earth's rotation causing day/night) allows judgment about whether any known counteracting cause exists and so supports extension beyond immediate adjacent cases; when causes are unknown, we lack assurance about unseen counteracting influences (example: bed-ridden savage and Niagara).

rubrics_metrics.name: Spatial extension of empirical laws requires shared individual agents/influence
rubrics_metrics.description: When an empirical law is extended beyond the local limits within which it has been found true by observation, the cases to which it is thus extended must be such as are presumably within the influence of the same individual agents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may extend empirical generalizations across space only where the same causes (or the same individual instance of a cause) plausibly operate (planetary example: if new planet revolves round the sun and is thus within the solar system's influence, we may infer it revolves on its axis). Expect greater extension when the origin is identical rather than merely similar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy as resemblance of relations can be as conclusive as induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Resemblance of Relations: when the circumstance in which two cases resemble each other can be shown to be the material circumstance (fundamentum relationis), an analogical argument may have the force of a rigorous induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the resemblance is precisely the circumstance on which all relevant consequences depend (e.g., management-by-a-committee relation), the analogical inference may be as conclusive as induction; otherwise it remains a weaker form of reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy (looser sense) reduces to: resemblance in some respects supports inference in others
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogical reasoning ... may be reduced to the following formula: Two things resemble each other in one or more respects; a certain proposition is true of the one; therefore it is true of the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This type of argument differs from complete induction because it lacks an established invariable conjunction between the shared properties and the inferred property; it provides a degree of probability rather than proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy requires that shared properties are not known to be unconnected with the inferred attribute
rubrics_metrics.description: To this argument it is of course requisite that the properties common to A with B shall be merely not known to be connected with m; they must not be properties known to be unconnected with it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If by elimination or deduction one can show the shared properties have nothing to do with the attribute m, the analogical argument is invalid. The supposition is that m depends on some unknown property of A, and B shares one or more of the remaining candidate properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every proved resemblance increases probability; every proved dissimilarity furnishes counter-probability
rubrics_metrics.description: Every such resemblance which can be pointed out between B and A, affords some degree of probability ... If every resemblance ... forms some additional reason for presuming that B has the attribute m; it is clear, è contra, that every dissimilarity which can be proved between them furnishes a counter-probability of the same nature on the other side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate analogical claims by weighing known agreements against known differences; differences that touch on indispensable conditions (for life, etc.) may overturn apparent favorable resemblances (moon/earth example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflicting analogies must be weighed against each other
rubrics_metrics.description: There may be a competition of conflicting analogies. The new case may be similar in some of its circumstances to cases in which the fact m exists, but in others to cases in which it is known not to exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When multiple analogies point in different directions (e.g., a painting resembles works of two different masters), decide which analogy is better supported by the relevant, material resemblances; absence of a decisive mark reduces the force of analogical inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strength of analogy depends on ascertained resemblance vs ascertained difference and unknown properties
rubrics_metrics.description: The value of an analogical argument ... depends on the extent of ascertained resemblance, compared first with the amount of ascertained difference, and next with the extent of the unexplored region of unascertained properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In close and extensive resemblance, analogy may approach valid induction (example: if B agrees with A in nine out of ten known properties, expect roughly nine-to-one probability for another derivative property). But when known elements are a small fraction of unknowns, even strong known resemblance is weak evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy is most valuable for adjacent cases in circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: The conclusions derived from analogy are only of any considerable value, when the case to which we reason is an adjacent case; adjacent ... in circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy is strongest when the new case shares the same conditions as prior cases; it is a guide-post pointing toward where to pursue more rigorous investigation and experiments rather than a final proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogical hypotheses are heuristically valuable but not substitutes for induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Considerations of analogy have the highest scientific value ... any suspicion, however slight, that sets an ingenious person at work to contrive an experiment ... may be of the greatest benefit to science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogies that suggest useful experiments or predict new facts are valuable even if not strictly true; hypotheses that explain many facts and predict others should be used to design 'experimenta crucis' but not accepted as positive truths without eventual induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausibility and successful prediction increase plausibility of hypothesis as guide
rubrics_metrics.description: If an hypothesis both explains known facts, and has led to the prediction of others previously unknown, and since verified by experience, the laws of the phenomenon ... must bear at least a great similarity to those of the class of phenomena to which the hypothesis assimilates it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A hypothesis's explanatory breadth and predictive success justify using it to suggest further experiments and tentatively treating its asserted analogies as likely; but one must avoid mistaking hypothesis for established truth as that can impede broader inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inductive methods presuppose the law of universal causation
rubrics_metrics.description: The validity of all the Inductive Methods depends on the assumption that every event, or the beginning of every phenomenon, must have some cause ... The universality of the law of causation is assumed in them all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methods such as Agreement and Difference implicitly assume that phenomena have antecedent causes; recognizing this assumption is necessary when evaluating inferences drawn by these methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Belief or instinct is not evidence for universal causation
rubrics_metrics.description: Belief is not proof, and does not dispense with the necessity of proof ... A mere strong association of ideas often causes a belief ... Evidence is not that which the mind does or must yield to, but that which it ought to yield to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept the universality of causation merely because it is widely or instinctively believed; appeals should be to sensory and factual faculties, not to merely psychological ubiquity of belief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal causation is itself an induction built from particular uniformities
rubrics_metrics.description: The belief we entertain in the universality ... of the law of cause and effect, is itself an instance of induction; ... We arrive at this universal law, by generalization from many laws of inferior generality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize circularity risk: inductive methods rely on the general law which was itself inferred inductively; accept it provisionally because it is grounded in accumulated particular uniformities, but be aware of its fallible origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction by simple enumeration is fallible but sometimes serviceable; trustworthiness varies with scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction per enumerationem simplicem ... is in reality the only kind of induction possible ... It would seem ... that induction by simple enumeration were an invalid process, no process grounded on it could be valid. But though a valid process, it is a fallible one ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple generalizations from observed absence of contrary instances are precarious, especially when generalized widely; nevertheless they have varying degrees of reliability (food nourishes, fire burns are examples). Scientific induction improves on them by replacing more fallible forms with less fallible ones (e.g., methods of difference/agreement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Precariousness of simple enumeration increases with breadth of generalization
rubrics_metrics.description: The precariousness of the method of simple enumeration is in an inverse ratio to the largeness of the generalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The wider and more ambitious a generalization, the less trustworthy mere enumeration becomes; this underlies rules for improving inductive inference by seeking tests from broader foundations of experience.
